findings.title: English reference file path is computed with a fragile regex that breaks for locale suffixes containing digits or hyphens
findings.body: The English bundle is located via `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class `[a-zA-Z-_]` does not include digits, so locale suffixes such as `messages_zh_CN.properties` (contains digits) or `messages_pt_BR.properties` (underscore is fine, but `zh_CN` is not matched by `[a-zA-Z-_]*` because of the digits) will not be replaced correctly. For `messages_zh_CN.properties` the regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` will match only `_CN.properties` (since `zh` is followed by `_`, which is in the class, but the digits `3`... actually `zh_CN` contains no digits; however locales like `messages_zh_CN.properties` are fine, but `messages_es_419.properties` or any locale with digits such as `messages_ca_ES_VALENCIA` or future `messages_zh_Hans_CN` would fail). More concretely, any locale code containing a digit (e.g. `messages_zh_CN` is fine, but `messages_hi_IN` is fine; the real problem is locales like `messages_pt_BR` are fine, but `messages_zh_TW` is fine — the actual breakage is for locales with digits like `messages_es_419` or `messages_en_US_POSIX`). When the replacement fails, the code tries to open a non-existent `_en.properties` path (e.g. `messages_zh_CN_en.properties` or a partially replaced name), causing a `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` that aborts verification of the entire file. This means the HTML sanitizer check silently fails (throws) for any translation file whose locale suffix contains a digit, instead of reporting illegal HTML. The path computation should use a robust method such as `file.getName().replaceFirst("_[^_]+(\\.[^_]+)*\\.properties$", "_en.properties")` or better, derive the English file from the parent directory and a fixed base name.

findings.title: HTML policy decision is based on a regex that misses uppercase tags and tags with attributes on the English source, allowing translations to inject arbitrary HTML
findings.body:
`containsHtml` uses `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` which only matches lowercase tag names. If the English source message contains an uppercase tag (e.g. `
`, `

`, ``), `containsHtml` returns false, so `POLICY_NO_HTML` is selected for the translation. However, the OWASP sanitizer's `POLICY_NO_HTML` strips all HTML, so a translation that legitimately needs to mirror an uppercase tag from the English source would be flagged as illegal — but more importantly, the policy selection is inconsistent: the sanitizer itself is case-insensitive for tag names, so an English message with `
` would be treated as "no HTML allowed" for translations, while the English message itself contains HTML. This is a correctness bug in the verifier's policy selection. Additionally, the regex `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` will not match tags like `` without attributes if written as `` (it requires at least one character after the tag name due to `[^>]*` being greedy but the `+` requires at least one letter — actually `` matches because `[a-z]+` matches `a` and `[^>]*` matches empty). The real issue is case sensitivity: HTML tag names are case-insensitive, so `
` in English source would not be detected, leading to `POLICY_NO_HTML` being applied to translations, which would then reject any `
` the translator adds. This causes false positives for translations of messages whose English source uses uppercase tags. The regex should be case-insensitive: `Pattern.compile("<[a-zA-Z]+[^>]*>")` or better `Pattern.compile("]*>")` to also catch closing tags.

findings.title: POLICY_SOME_HTML allows only br, p, strong, b but the anchor sanitization removes anchors before sanitization, meaning anchor tags are never actually validated by the HTML policy
findings.body: The `POLICY_SOME_HTML` policy allows only `br`, `p`, `strong`, `b` — it does not allow `a` tags. However, the code first calls `santizeAnchors(key, value, englishValue)` which removes matching anchor tags from the value before sanitization (line 88). This means anchor tags are stripped from the value before the sanitizer runs, so the sanitizer never sees them and cannot validate their attributes (e.g., `href` values). A malicious translation could include an anchor tag with a `javascript:` href or an `onclick` attribute; `santizeAnchors` would remove the entire anchor tag from the value (if it matches the English anchor), so the sanitizer would not flag it. But if the anchor does NOT match the English anchor, `santizeAnchors` adds a message and breaks, but the value still contains the unmatched anchor, which the sanitizer (POLICY_SOME_HTML) would strip because `a` is not allowed. However, the design intent seems to be that anchors should be allowed if they match the English source. Since POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `a`, any anchor that survives `santizeAnchors` (i.e., matched anchors are removed, unmatched anchors cause a message but remain in the value) will be stripped by the sanitizer, causing a false "Illegal HTML" report for legitimate matching anchors. The policy should explicitly allow `a` with safe attributes (e.g., `href`) when the English source contains anchors, or the anchor handling should be integrated into the policy. As written, the verifier will report false positives for any translation that contains an anchor tag matching the English source, because the anchor is removed before sanitization but the sanitizer would have stripped it anyway — actually the anchor is removed, so the sanitized value won't contain it, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` will detect the removal as a difference, reporting "Illegal HTML" for a perfectly valid translation. This is a bug: legitimate anchor tags in translations are falsely flagged.

findings.title: santizeAnchors method name is misspelled and the anchor matching logic is flawed for multiple anchors
findings.body: The method `santizeAnchors` (line 150) is misspelled (should be `sanitizeAnchors`). More importantly, the logic for matching anchors between translation and English is incorrect when there are multiple anchors: it uses two independent matchers (`matcher` on the translation value and `englishMatcher` on the English value) and calls `englishMatcher.find()` inside the loop. If the translation has anchors in a different order than the English source, the matching will fail incorrectly. For example, if English has `text1 ... text2` and the translation reverses the order, the first translation anchor will be compared to the first English anchor, fail, and report "Didn't find anchor tag" even though both anchors exist. The correct approach is to collect all anchor tags from the English value into a multiset (or list) and check that each translation anchor exists in that collection, removing matched ones. The current sequential matching assumes anchors appear in the same order, which is not guaranteed for translations.

findings.title: Anchor removal uses replaceFirst with the English matcher's group, which may remove the wrong occurrence if the same anchor tag appears multiple times
findings.body: In `santizeAnchors`, when a translation anchor matches an English anchor, the code does `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. This removes the first occurrence of that exact anchor tag string from the value. If the same anchor tag (e.g., `<a href="https://example.com">`) appears multiple times in the translation, only the first occurrence is removed, but the loop continues with the next translation anchor. If there are duplicate identical anchors, the matching logic breaks: the second identical translation anchor will be compared to the next English anchor (which may be different), causing a false mismatch. Additionally, `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence in the entire value, which may not correspond to the anchor found by `matcher.find()` if there are earlier identical strings. This can lead to incorrect anchor removal and false "Illegal HTML" reports or missed detection of changed anchors.

findings.title: Unconditional unescapeHtml4 on sanitized value can reintroduce HTML entities that were intentionally escaped in the source, causing false mismatches
findings.body: After sanitization, the code does `sanitized = org.apache.commons.text.StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(sanitized)` (line 95) to reverse the sanitizer's HTML entity escaping. However, the original value is also unescaped in `normalizeValue` (line 130). If the original message intentionally contains an HTML entity like `&` that should remain escaped in the output (e.g., to display a literal `&`), the sanitizer will escape it to `&amp;`, then `unescapeHtml4` will convert it back to `&`, which matches the normalized original. But if the original contains a literal `&` (i.e., the text "&" as displayed), the sanitizer escapes the `&` to `&amp;`, and unescapeHtml4 converts it to `&`, which matches. The issue is that `unescapeHtml4` is applied unconditionally, which can mask actual differences: if the sanitizer escapes a `<` to `<`, unescapeHtml4 converts it back to `<`, making the sanitized value appear unchanged even though the sanitizer altered it. This defeats the purpose of detecting illegal HTML: a translation containing `<script>` would be sanitized to `<script>`, then unescaped back to `<script>`, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` would see no difference, so the illegal HTML would NOT be reported. This is a critical flaw: the unescape step completely undermines the sanitizer's detection of disallowed tags. The comment says "Sanitizer will escape HTML entities for quotes and also for numeric tags like '<1>'", but the unescape reverses ALL entity escaping, including for `<` and `>`, making the check ineffective for detecting stripped tags.

findings.title: Removing "<!-- -->" after sanitization is a hack that may not cover all sanitizer artifacts for double curly braces
findings.body: The code does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "")` to remove artifacts the sanitizer inserts for double curly braces (e.g., `{{name}}`). However, the OWASP sanitizer may produce different artifacts depending on the context (e.g., `<!-- -->` may appear with different spacing or as `<!--  -->`). If the sanitizer's output format changes or if the artifact appears differently, this replacement will fail, causing false "Illegal HTML" reports for messages containing `{{...}}` placeholders. This is fragile and should be replaced with a more robust normalization, such as replacing the sanitizer's comment artifacts with a regex like `<!--\s*-->`.

findings.title: normalizeValue special-case for templateHelp uses regex that only matches uppercase letters, missing lowercase claim names
findings.body: In `normalizeValue`, for the key `templateHelp`, the code does `value.replaceAll("CLAIM\\.<[A-Z]*>", "")`. This regex only matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` where NAME consists solely of uppercase letters. If the actual message contains a claim name with lowercase letters (e.g., `CLAIM.<sub>` or `CLAIM.<email>`), the regex will not match, and the `<sub>` will be treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, causing a false "Illegal HTML" report. The regex should be `CLAIM\\.<[A-Za-z0-9_]*>` or similar to match typical claim names.

findings.title: normalizeValue choice-format replacement regex does not handle nested braces in choice patterns
findings.body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` or `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `...`. The regex `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, but choice formats can contain nested braces (e.g., `{0,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` has no nested braces, but more complex patterns like `{0,choice,0#{1,choice,1#one|1<many}}` would break). For the current messages, this works, but it is fragile. A more robust approach would be to use a proper MessageFormat parser or a balanced-brace matcher.

findings.title: Email RTL style removal checks file path for "email" but the path may not contain "email" for all email theme directories
findings.body: The code checks `file.getAbsolutePath().contains("email")` to decide whether to strip ` style="direction: rtl;"` from values. This is fragile: if the email theme directory is named differently (e.g., `emails` or a custom theme path), the check fails. More importantly, the RTL style attribute is part of the HTML and should be handled by the sanitizer policy (e.g., allowing `style` on specific elements) rather than being stripped via string replacement. The current approach also only strips the exact string ` style="direction: rtl;"` — if the attribute uses single quotes or different spacing, it won't be stripped, causing false positives. This should be replaced with a proper policy that allows the `style` attribute with the specific RTL value, or the normalization should be more robust.

findings.title: Test verifyNoHtmlAllowed uses noHtml_de.properties but the English reference noHtml_en.properties has no HTML, so the test does not verify that HTML is rejected when English has no HTML
findings.body: The test `verifyNoHtmlAllowed` loads `noHtml_de.properties` which contains `key=Some HTML`, and expects an "Illegal HTML" message. However, the English reference file `noHtml_en.properties` contains `key=No HTML` (no HTML tags). The verifier's logic selects `POLICY_NO_HTML` when the English value contains no HTML (via `containsHtml`). So the test does verify that HTML in the translation is rejected when English has no HTML. But the test name and fixture naming are confusing: `noHtml_de` suggests the German file has no HTML, but it actually has HTML. The test would be clearer if the German file were named `htmlInTranslation_de.properties` or similar. More importantly, there is no test for the case where the English source contains HTML and the translation also contains HTML (should be allowed), or where the English contains HTML but the translation contains a different disallowed tag (should be rejected). The test suite lacks coverage for the positive case (HTML allowed when English has HTML) and for the anchor matching logic.

findings.title: Test verifyNoChangedAnchors does not verify that matching anchors are allowed (positive case)
findings.body: The test `verifyNoChangedAnchors` loads `changedAnchor_de.properties` (which has `<a href="http://malicious.com">`) and `changedAnchor_en.properties` (which has `<a href="http://example.com">`), and expects a "Didn't find anchor tag" message. This tests the negative case (changed anchor detected). However, there is no test for the positive case: a translation with an anchor that exactly matches the English anchor should NOT produce any message. Without this test, a regression that incorrectly flags matching anchors as errors would not be caught. Given the complexity of the anchor matching logic (see other findings), a positive test is essential.

findings.title: Account UI error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} (React i18next format) to {0}/{1}/{2} (MessageFormat), breaking the frontend's interpolation

The new format uses single braces `{0}` with Java MessageFormat choice syntax, which is the format used by the server-side FreeMarker templates. The account UI (React) will not correctly interpolate `{0}` — it expects `{{0}}`. This change breaks the error message display in the account console: the placeholders will not be replaced with actual values, and the `{2,choice,...}` syntax will be displayed literally. The account UI messages should retain the `{{0}}` format, or the frontend should be updated to support MessageFormat. This is an API/contract break between the message resource format and the frontend's i18n library.

findings.title: OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer version 20240325.1 is used without a specific scope, potentially bundling it into the plugin's runtime
findings.body: In `misc/theme-verifier/pom.xml`, the dependency `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1` is declared without a `<scope>` element, meaning it defaults to `compile` scope. Since this is a Maven plugin (`<packaging>maven-plugin</packaging>`), compile-scope dependencies are included in the plugin's classpath. This is fine for a build-time verification tool, but it's worth noting that the sanitizer library and its transitive dependencies (e.g., Guava) will be bundled. For a build tool, this is acceptable. However, the version `20240325.1` is a dated snapshot; it's recommended to use a stable release version if available, or at least document why this specific version is chosen. Not a blocking issue.

findings.title: verify() method catches IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml throws RuntimeException for IO errors, which is not caught and propagates as unchecked exception
findings.body: The `verify()` method (line 46) wraps `Files.readString` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys` in a try-catch for `IOException`, throwing `MojoExecutionException`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` (called at line 51) catches `IOException` internally and throws `RuntimeException` (lines 70, 79). This `RuntimeException` is not caught by the `verify()` method's catch block (which only catches `IOException`), so it propagates as an unchecked exception. In a Maven plugin context, an uncaught `RuntimeException` will cause the build to fail with a stack trace rather than a clean `MojoExecutionException` message. The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or the `verify()` method should catch `RuntimeException` as well. This inconsistency in error handling makes the plugin's error reporting inconsistent.

findings.title: PropertyResourceBundle is loaded twice for the same file (once in verify() via Files.readString, once in verifySafeHtml via FileInputStream)
findings.body: The `verify()` method reads the file contents with `Files.readString(file.toPath())` for duplicate key checking, and then `verifySafeHtml()` opens the same file again with `new FileInputStream(file)` to create a `PropertyResourceBundle`. The file is read twice from disk. For large property files, this is inefficient. The `PropertyResourceBundle` could be created once and reused, or the duplicate key check could be performed on the bundle's keys. This is a minor performance issue, not critical for a build-time tool.

findings.title: HTML_TAGS regex does not match closing tags or self-closing tags, so containsHtml may return false for English messages that only contain closing tags
findings.body:
The `HTML_TAGS` pattern is `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` (line 139). This matches opening tags like `
`, `

`, but does NOT match closing tags like `

` or `` because the pattern requires `<` followed by `[a-z]+` (letters only), and `

` has a `/` after `<`. If an English message contains only a closing tag (unlikely but possible, e.g., a message that is just `

`), `containsHtml` would return false, and `POLICY_NO_HTML` would be applied to translations, causing false positives. More realistically, if an English message contains `
` (self-closing), the pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` matches `
` because `[^>]*` matches `/`. But for closing tags, the pattern fails. The pattern should be `]*>` to match both opening and closing tags, and should be case-insensitive.

findings.title: ANCHOR_PATTERN regex `</?a[^>]*>` does not match uppercase `<A>` tags and may match `<address>` or other tags starting with 'a'
findings.body: The `ANCHOR_PATTERN` is `Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>")` (line 145). This pattern matches `<a...>` and `</a...>` but has two issues: (1) it is case-sensitive, so `<A HREF=...>` (uppercase) would not be matched; (2) it matches any tag starting with `a`, such as `<address>`, `<abbr>`, `<article>`, etc., because `[^>]*` matches the rest of the tag name. For example, `<address>` would be matched as an anchor tag, leading to incorrect anchor detection. The pattern should be `</?a\s[^>]*>|</?a>` to match only `a` tags (with optional attributes) or use a word boundary: `</?a\b[^>]*>`.

findings.title: Czech error-invalid-multivalued-size uses a complex choice format that may not be grammatically correct for all numbers
findings.body: In `themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/login/messages/messages_cs.properties`, the value for `error-invalid-multivalued-size` is `Atribut {0} musí mít nejméně {1} {1,choice,0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot} a nejvíce {2} {2,choice,0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot}.` — this uses a Czech plural choice format. The Czech plural rules are: 1 → nominative singular, 2-4 → nominative plural, 0/5+ → genitive plural. The pattern `0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot` maps: 0 → `hodnot` (genitive plural), 1 → `hodnotu` (accusative singular? should be `hodnota` for nominative singular after "nejméně"?), 2-4 → `hodnoty` (nominative plural), 5+ → `hodnot` (genitive plural). The form `hodnotu` for 1 is accusative singular, but after "nejméně" (at least), Czech typically uses genitive: "neznéně jedné hodnoty" (genitive singular). So `1#hodnotu` may be grammatically incorrect — it should be `1#hodnoty` (genitive singular). This is a translation quality issue. The verifier will not catch this because it replaces the choice pattern with `...`. Not a blocking issue for the PR, but worth noting.

findings.title: Error message substring extraction can produce confusing output when start/end indices overlap or exceed string lengths
findings.body: In the error reporting code (lines 101-111), the start and end indices are computed to strip common prefix/suffix, then `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` are used. If `start + end > value.length()` (which can happen if the strings are very different), `value.length() - end` could be less than `start`, causing a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. For example, if `value = "abc"` and `sanitized = "xyz"`, start would be 0 (no common prefix), end would be 0 (no common suffix), so `value.substring(0, 3)` is fine. But if `value = "a"` and `sanitized = "b"`, start=0, end=0, fine. The dangerous case is when the strings share a long common prefix and suffix that overlap: e.g., `value = "aaa"` and `sanitized = "aa"`, start would advance to 2 (common prefix "aa"), end would advance to 1 (common suffix "a"), then `value.substring(2, 3-1=2)` → `substring(2,2)` → empty string, and `sanitized.substring(2, 2-1=1)` → `substring(2,1)` → `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` because start > end. This would crash the verifier with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should guard against `start + end > length` by clamping or using `Math.min`.
